title: The Fake Photo That Helped Sink a U.S. Senator
summary: The Fake Photo That Helped Sink a U.S. Senator
detailed: In the last stretch of the 1950 Maryland Senate race, roughly 300,000 copies of a four-page tabloid called From the Record went out across the state, and inside was a picture of Senator Millard Tydings standing close beside Earl Browder, the former head of the American Communist Party.
What went into the Tydings picture were two real news photographs, and the Senate report is precise about them.

sentences: In the last stretch of the 1950 Maryland Senate race, roughly 300,000 copies of a four-page tabloid called From the Record went out across the state, and inside was a picture of Senator Millard Tydings standing close beside Earl Browder, the former head of the American Communist Party.
The two men had never posed together, and the caption underneath called the picture a composite.
Tydings lost by more than 43,000 votes.
A composite in 1950 was scissors, paste, an airbrush, and a copy camera.
Someone cut a figure out of one print, positioned it on another, worked the seam down with retouching, and then photographed the whole assembly to make a fresh negative.
From that negative forward, the picture behaved like any other photograph.
There was no layer stack to inspect and no file to interrogate.
The evidence of assembly lived on a paste-up board that stayed in the art department.
Newsprint then removed whatever traces survived.
A continuous-tone print has to be broken into halftone dots before it can go on a press, and newspaper screens were coarse.
Fine edge detail, the exact thing that would reveal a cut line or an airbrushed transition, is the first thing a coarse screen throws away.
By the time the picture reached a Maryland kitchen table, it was a field of dots on cheap paper, and the seam that a retoucher had worried over was simply gone.
What went into the Tydings picture were two real news photographs, and the Senate report is precise about them.
One was a 1938 photograph of Tydings, taken while he listened to election returns.
The other was a 1950 photograph of Browder made at the very hearings the tabloid was attacking, trimmed, reversed left to right by rephotographing, and fitted against him.
Assembled, they produced an image of two men in what looks like an easy private conversation, Browder talking, Tydings listening.
The Washington Times-Herald did the work.
Assistant Managing Editor Garvin E.
Tankersley, who ordered the composite made, later told a Senate subcommittee that he had been trying to "show that Mr.
Browder with kid gloves," according to Time's account of the hearings .
Asked whether he saw anything wrong with the picture, he said he did not.
The tabloid ran the word composite in the caption anyway.
Tydings had spent the spring of 1950 chairing the Senate subcommittee that examined Joseph McCarthy's claim that the State Department was riddled with Communists.
The hearings ran from March into July, and the majority report described McCarthy's charges as a fraud and a hoax.
McCarthy went after Tydings' seat that fall.
Browder is the reason the picture had any grip at all.
He had led the Communist Party in the United States through the 1930s and into the war years, and by 1950 he had been expelled from it, which made him a convenient figure for both sides to summon.
He appeared before Tydings' subcommittee during those hearings, and the damning part is that the Times-Herald had photographs of it.
Nothing in the frame was invented except the thing that mattered: the distance between two men.
The mechanics came out later under oath.
Ruth "Bazy" Miller, who published the Times-Herald, testified that McCarthy had asked her to print the tabloid and that she handed the job to her chief editorial writer, Frank M.

Smith, who defended the picture as "not a fake" and "not a fraud," said McCarthy's office supplied much of the story material, and he left his newspaper job afterward to work for the man who won the election.
The tabloid itself claimed to be published and paid for by a group called Young Democrats for Butler.
Republican John Marshall Butler beat Tydings roughly 53 percent to 46 percent, ending a Senate career that had started in 1927.
Tydings filed a complaint with the Rules Committee in December 1950.
Butler was seated without prejudice on January 3, 1951, while the investigation went forward, public hearings ran from February 20 to April 11, and the committee report came out on August 20, 1951.
The story is usually retold as a straightforward forgery: McCarthy's people faked a photograph, passed it off as genuine, and stole an election with it.
That version is wrong in two specific places.
The picture was not passed off as an unaltered photograph.

Time, reporting on the 1951 hearings, wrote that the caption labeled the picture "composite." The disclosure was printed on the same page as the image, in the ordinary place a reader would look for a credit line, and it did not save Tydings.
The second is what the Senate actually did.
The Subcommittee on Privileges and Elections condemned the campaign in unusually direct language and then declined to act on it.

Its findings called From the Record a publication containing "misleading half truths, misrepresentations, and false innuendos that maliciously and without foundation attack the loyalty and patriotism" of Tydings, a man who had won the Distinguished Service Cross in World War I.

On the picture itself, the subcommittee wrote that it could never have been the intention of the framers of the First Amendment to allow, under the guise of freedom of the press, the publication of any portrayal of the character of the composite picture as it appeared in the tabloid.

The subcommittee also found that Young Democrats for Butler was a false front, that the tabloid was neither published nor paid for by that group, and that McCarthy had made his own staff available for research, pictures, composition, and printing.
Butler's campaign manager, Jon M.
Jonkel, was indicted, pleaded guilty, and was sentenced for violating Maryland election law.

The report found insufficient basis to recommend unseating him, largely because the Senate had no established standard of campaign conduct to measure him against, and it asked the Rules Committee to write one.

The full record of the case sits on the Senate's own page for the contested election, and the findings themselves were quoted at length in an August 1951 Senate resolution seeking McCarthy's expulsion, reprinted in a later Senate investigation of McCarthy.
A photograph and its caption do not arrive at the same speed.
The picture registers as a scene in well under a second, before any text is read, and it registers as a memory of an event rather than as an argument to be evaluated.
The caption arrives second, as a smaller, slower, optional thing.
Reversing that order requires the reader to go back and revise an impression that already feels like something they saw.
The word chosen made it worse.
"Composite" in 1950 was printing-trade vocabulary.
To a picture editor, it meant two negatives combined.
To a voter in Cumberland, it meant close to nothing, and nothing in the layout translated it.
A line reading that these two men were never photographed together, and that this picture was two separate photographs pasted into one, would have been a disclosure.
A technical term set in small type under a convincing halftone was a legal hedge dressed as one.
The distribution finished the job.
